title: How to start investing if you're self-employed in the US
description: Building a retirement plan without an HR department: Solo 401(k)s and SEP IRAs.
content:
When you leave the W-2 world to become your own boss, you gain freedom but lose infrastructure. There is no HR department to set up your 401(k), and no employer to match your contributions. As a result, many self-employed Americans fall behind on retirement savings. The irony is that the US tax code actually offers *better* retirement perks for the self-employed than for employees—if you know which accounts to open. This guide explains how to build a DIY benefits package that rivals a Fortune 500 company.

Key Takeaways

  • The Solo 401(k) Advantage: This is the gold standard. It allows you to contribute as both employee ($23k) and employer (20% of profit), with a massive total cap ($69k+).
  • The SEP IRA Simplicity: Easier to set up than a Solo 401(k) but lacks the 'Catch-Up' contribution for older savers and doesn't allow loans.
  • Automated Taxes: Investing is impossible if you owe the IRS. You must segregate 30% of every invoice for taxes *before* investing.
  • Roth Options: Solo 401(k)s can have a Roth component, allowing for tax-free growth on your massive contributions.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Self-employed individuals pay the full 15.3% FICA tax (Self-Employment Tax). Using tax-deferred retirement accounts reduces your income tax, but not the SE tax. However, the ability to shelter up to $69,000 (2025 limit) from income tax is a massive wealth accelerator.

Choosing Your Vehicle

You are the CEO and the Janitor. You choose the plan.

1. Solo 401(k) (The Heavy Lifter)

Best For: Solopreneurs with no staff (except spouse) who want to maximize savings.

  • Contribution: Up to $23,000 as employee + ~20% of net business profit as employer.
  • Pros: High limits, Roth option, Loan option.
  • Cons: Requires EIN. More paperwork (Form 5500) once balance exceeds $250k.

2. SEP IRA (The Easy Button)

Best For: Freelancers who want zero paperwork.

  • Contribution: ~20-25% of net profit. No 'Employee' fixed amount.
  • Pros: Set up in 5 minutes at Fidelity/Vanguard.
  • Cons: If you hire employees later, you MUST contribute to their SEP too (expensive). No Roth option usually.

3. SIMPLE IRA

Best For: Small businesses with a few employees.

Lower contribution limits than the Solo 401(k) but easier to administer for small teams.

The 'Pay Yourself' Workflow

  1. Open the Account: Don't wait until tax time. Open the Solo 401(k) by Dec 31 to secure the deduction for the year.
  2. The 'Net' Percentage: Decide on a flat percentage of Net Profit (e.g., 10%) to invest. Transfer this monthly.
  3. The 'Employer Match' Hack: At the end of the year, calculate your total profit. Write yourself a 'Bonus' contribution check from the business to the 401(k) to max out the Employer portion.
  4. Automate to Roth IRA: In addition to the business accounts, you can still have a personal Roth IRA. Set up a $583/mo auto-draft from your personal checking.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I have a Solo 401(k) if I have a day job?

Yes, but the 'Employee' limit ($23,500) is shared across all jobs. If you max it at your day job, your side hustle Solo 401(k) can only receive 'Employer' profit-sharing contributions.

Do I need an LLC?

No. A Sole Proprietorship works fine. You just need an EIN (Employer Identification Number) from the IRS, which is free.

What if my income varies?

That's why the Solo 401(k) is great. You are not required to contribute every year. In bad years, you can contribute $0. In good years, you shovel it in.
